claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the correlation analysis between neural activity and behavior.

claims.claim: Pharmacological inactivation of the PPTg causally affected behavior by decreasing the influence of recent choices on upcoming choices.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that these representations influenced action selection: the probability of particular upcoming choices was predictably related to the firing rates of neurons selective for choice on the previous trial, and pharmacological inactivation of the PPTg causally affected behavior, in part by decreasing the influence of recent choices on upcoming choices.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the pharmacological manipulation experiments.

claims.claim: Mice tended to choose the left port more often when they had chosen the left port on the previous trial and had been rewarded.
claims.source: As illustrated in the example data from one mouse in Figure 1B,C, the mouse tended to choose the left port more often when it had chosen the left port on the previous trial and had been rewarded (Figure 1B, compare solid black line to gray line), and tended to choose the right port more often when it had chosen the right port on the previous trial whether or not it had been rewarded (Figure 1C, compare solid and dashed black lines to gray line).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis, illustrated in Figure 1B,C.

claims.claim: Mice tended to choose the right port more often when they had chosen the right port on the previous trial whether or not they had been rewarded.
claims.source: As illustrated in the example data from one mouse in Figure 1B,C, the mouse tended to choose the left port more often when it had chosen the left port on the previous trial and had been rewarded (Figure 1B, compare solid black line to gray line), and tended to choose the right port more often when it had chosen the right port on the previous trial whether or not it had been rewarded (Figure 1C, compare solid and dashed black lines to gray line).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Mice tended to choose the same side as they had on the previous trial.
claims.source: Consistent with the example data shown in Figure 1B,C, and with some previous work (Lau and Glimcher, 2005), we found that, while there was some variability across mice, they tended to choose the same side as they had on the previous trial (reflected in positive values of  β Choice1) [although in different tasks, a tendency to choose the opposite side has been observed (Lau and Glimcher, 2005; Kim et al., 2007; Sul et al., 2011)], and that this tendency was enhanced when the mouse was rewarded on the previous trial (reflected in positive values of β Outcome: L1 and negative values of β Outcome: R1; Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis using logistic regression, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The tendency to choose the same side as on the previous trial was enhanced when the mouse was rewarded on the previous trial.
claims.source: Consistent with the example data shown in Figure 1B,C, and with some previous work (Lau and Glimcher, 2005), we found that, while there was some variability across mice, they tended to choose the same side as they had on the previous trial (reflected in positive values of  β Choice1) [although in different tasks, a tendency to choose the opposite side has been observed (Lau and Glimcher, 2005; Kim et al., 2007; Sul et al., 2011)], and that this tendency was enhanced when the mouse was rewarded on the previous trial (reflected in positive values of β Outcome: L1 and negative values of β Outcome: R1; Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral analysis using logistic regression, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Including the choice and outcome on the previous trial improved the predictive accuracy of the behavioral model for five of seven mice.
claims.source: We found that including the choice and outcome on the previous trial improved the predictive accuracy of the model for five of seven mice (Figure 1E, p<0.0001, one-tailed paired Student's t test separately by mouse).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison analysis, illustrated in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Including the choice and outcome from two trials back did not further improve the predictive accuracy of the model in any mice.
claims.source: However, including the choice and outcome from two trials back did not further improve the predictive accuracy of the model in any mice (Figure 1F, p>0.16, one-tailed paired Student's t test).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison analysis, illustrated in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Movement duration did not depend on the previous choice in most cases.
claims.source: However, we found that this was not the case (durations for rightward movements preceded by right choices and preceded by left choices, analyzed separately for each mouse, did not differ in 7/7 mice; durations for leftward movements preceded by right choices and preceded by left choices did not differ in 6/7 mice; p>0.05, two-tailed unpaired Students t-tests separately by mouse).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of movement duration.

claims.claim: Choices in the task are influenced by what happened on the previous trial, primarily by the choice rather than the outcome.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that choices in our task are influenced by what happened on the previous trial – primarily by the choice rather than the outcome – and little influenced by the choice or the outcome from two trials in the past.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the behavioral analyses.

claims.claim: Choices in the task are little influenced by the choice or outcome from two trials in the past.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that choices in our task are influenced by what happened on the previous trial – primarily by the choice rather than the outcome – and little influenced by the choice or the outcome from two trials in the past.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the behavioral analyses.

claims.claim: Few PPTg neurons exhibited a preference for choice on the current trial during the pre-stimulus epoch.
claims.source: We found that few neurons exhibited a preference for choice during this epoch (Figure 2, p<0.05, Monte Carlo permutation test).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the preference analysis of neural data, illustrated in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Few PPTg neurons exhibited outcome preference during the pre-stimulus epoch.
claims.source: We found that few neurons exhibited outcome preference (Figure 2, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the preference analysis of neural data, illustrated in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: A sizeable fraction of PPTg neurons exhibited a preference for the choice on the previous trial during the pre-stimulus epoch.
claims.source: Across the population, a sizeable fraction of neurons exhibited a preference for the choice (Figure 2G; 26% preferred ipsilateral, 49% preferred contralateral, p<0.05; more preferred contralateral than ipsilateral, p=0.001, χ2 test) and outcome (Figure 2H; 46% were selective, p<0.05) on the previous trial.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the preference analysis of neural data, illustrated in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: A sizeable fraction of PPTg neurons exhibited a preference for the outcome on the previous trial during the pre-stimulus epoch.
claims.source: Across the population, a sizeable fraction of neurons exhibited a preference for the choice (Figure 2G; 26% preferred ipsilateral, 49% preferred contralateral, p<0.05; more preferred contralateral than ipsilateral, p=0.001, χ2 test) and outcome (Figure 2H; 46% were selective, p<0.05) on the previous trial.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the preference analysis of neural data, illustrated in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: More PPTg neurons preferred contralateral than ipsilateral choices on the previous trial.
claims.source: Across the population, a sizeable fraction of neurons exhibited a preference for the choice (Figure 2G; 26% preferred ipsilateral, 49% preferred contralateral, p<0.05; more preferred contralateral than ipsilateral, p=0.001, χ2 test) and outcome (Figure 2H; 46% were selective, p<0.05) on the previous trial.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the preference analysis of neural data, illustrated in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: There is a modest correlation between preference for the choice on the previous and current trials.
claims.source: We found a modest correlation between preference for the choice on the previous (Figure 2G) and current (Figure 2C) trials (r = 0.25, p=1.42 × 10−8).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis of neural preferences.

claims.claim: Two-thirds of PPTg neurons maintained their preference for which reward port was chosen during movement to and from the reward port.
claims.source: We found that, rather than representing movement direction, two-thirds of neurons maintained their preference for which reward port was chosen (p=9.12 × 10−6, χ2 test), suggesting that the preference of PPTg neurons for previous choice (Figure 2G) cannot be accounted for by a dependence on movement direction.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of neural activity during movements in opposite directions.

claims.claim: The preference of PPTg neurons for previous choice cannot be accounted for by a dependence on movement direction.
claims.source: We found that, rather than representing movement direction, two-thirds of neurons maintained their preference for which reward port was chosen (p=9.12 × 10−6, χ2 test), suggesting that the preference of PPTg neurons for previous choice (Figure 2G) cannot be accounted for by a dependence on movement direction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of neural activity during movements in opposite directions.

claims.claim: Few PPTg neurons exhibited a preference for choice or outcome two trials back during the pre-stimulus epoch.
claims.source: We then calculated choice and outcome preference with respect to two trials back (Figure 2I–L) and found that, as was the case for the current trial, few neurons exhibited a preference for choice (Figure 2K) or outcome (Figure 2L), consistent with the relatively little influence on behavior of the choice and outcome from two trials in the past (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the preference analysis of neural data, illustrated in Figure 2K,L.

claims.claim: A larger proportion of PPTg neurons exhibited a preference for choice or outcome one trial back than on either the current trial or two trials back.
claims.source: Thus, a larger proportion of neurons exhibited a preference for choice or outcome one trial back than on either the current trial or two trials back (choice, p=2.0 × 10–48; outcome, p=3.0 × 10–5, Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA; post-hoc comparisons: choice, one trial back vs. current trial, p=5.6 × 10–30; one trial back vs. two trials back, p=1.6 × 10–30; outcome, one trial back vs. current trial, p=4.0 × 10–4; one trial back vs. two trials back, p=0.002), and there were no differences between the fractions of neurons exhibiting a preference for choice or outcome on the current trial and two trials back (choice, two trials back vs. current trial, p=0.92; outcome, two trials back vs. current trial, p = 0.99).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the statistical comparison of neural preferences across different trial lags.

claims.claim: There were no differences between the fractions of PPTg neurons exhibiting a preference for choice or outcome on the current trial and two trials back.
claims.source: Thus, a larger proportion of neurons exhibited a preference for choice or outcome one trial back than on either the current trial or two trials back (choice, p=2.0 × 10–48; outcome, p=3.0 × 10–5, Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA; post-hoc comparisons: choice, one trial back vs. current trial, p=5.6 × 10–30; one trial back vs. two trials back, p=1.6 × 10–30; outcome, one trial back vs. current trial, p=4.0 × 10–4; one trial back vs. two trials back, p=0.002), and there were no differences between the fractions of neurons exhibiting a preference for choice or outcome on the current trial and two trials back (choice, two trials back vs. current trial, p=0.92; outcome, two trials back vs. current trial, p = 0.99).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the statistical comparison of neural preferences across different trial lags.

claims.claim: PPTg activity during the pre-stimulus epoch is primarily modulated by the choice and outcome on the previous trial.
claims.source: These results suggest that PPTg activity during the pre-stimulus epoch is primarily modulated by the choice and outcome on the previous trial (although our analyses again cannot entirely rule out the possibility that body position also modulates neural activity).
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the preference analyses, with a caveat about body position.

claims.claim: PPTg activity in epochs other than the pre-stimulus epoch reflects the choice and outcome on the current trial.
claims.source: Previous work using the same task has shown that PPTg activity in other epochs reflects the choice and outcome on the current trial (Thompson and Felsen, 2013), consistent with other studies of PPTg function (Matsumura et al., 1997; Dormont et al., 1998; Kobayashi et al., 2002; Norton et al., 2011; Maclaren et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The influence of the previous trial on PPTg activity declines by the time the mouse exits the odor port.
claims.source: The influence of the previous trial declines by the time the mouse exits the odor port (Figure 3A, middle), and the influence of the current choice increases upon reward port entry (Figure 3A, right), consistent with the fact that many neurons exhibit preference for the current choice during and following entrance to the reward port (Thompson and Felsen, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The influence of the current choice on PPTg activity increases upon reward port entry.
claims.source: The influence of the previous trial declines by the time the mouse exits the odor port (Figure 3A, middle), and the influence of the current choice increases upon reward port entry (Figure 3A, right), consistent with the fact that many neurons exhibit preference for the current choice during and following entrance to the reward port (Thompson and Felsen, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Initially, even preceding odor delivery, the activity of many PPTg neurons reflects the choice on the previous trial, while the activity of virtually no neurons reflects the choice on the current trial.
claims.source: Initially – even preceding odor delivery – the activity of many neurons reflects the choice on the previous trial, while the activity of virtually no neurons reflects the choice on the current trial (Figure 3C, left).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: During stimulus presentation many PPTg neurons begin to reflect the choice on the current trial.
claims.source: During stimulus presentation many neurons begin to reflect the choice on the current trial, and by the time the movement is initiated more neurons reflect the choice on the current than the previous trial (Figure 3C, middle).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: By the time the movement is initiated more PPTg neurons reflect the choice on the current than the previous trial.
claims.source: During stimulus presentation many neurons begin to reflect the choice on the current trial, and by the time the movement is initiated more neurons reflect the choice on the current than the previous trial (Figure 3C, middle).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The choice on the current trial retains its influence on PPTg activity for the remainder of the trial while the influence of the choice on the previous trial declines.
claims.source: The choice on the current trial retains its influence for the remainder of the trial while the influence of the choice on the previous trial declines (Figure 3C, right), although, interestingly, a sizeable fraction of neurons continues to reflect the choice on the previous trial until well-after the mouse has made its choice on the current trial.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: A sizeable fraction of PPTg neurons continues to reflect the choice on the previous trial until well-after the mouse has made its choice on the current trial.
claims.source: The choice on the current trial retains its influence for the remainder of the trial while the influence of the choice on the previous trial declines (Figure 3C, right), although, interestingly, a sizeable fraction of neurons continues to reflect the choice on the previous trial until well-after the mouse has made its choice on the current trial.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The activity of more PPTg neurons is more strongly influenced by previous trial outcome early in the trial, and by current trial outcome later in the trial.
claims.source: Similar to the evolving representation of choice, the activity of more neurons is more strongly influenced by previous trial outcome early in the trial (Figure 3D,E, left), and by current trial outcome later in the trial (Figure 3D,E, right).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3D,E.

claims.claim: Virtually no PPTg neurons represent previous outcome by the time the mouse initiates its movement to the reward port.
claims.source: In contrast to the long-lasting representation of previous choice (Figure 3B,C), virtually none of these neurons represent previous outcome by the time the mouse initiates its movement to the reward port (Figure 3D,E, middle; however, note that the population of neurons analyzed was selected based on preference for previous choice, and not previous outcome, during the pre-stimulus epoch).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis of neural data over time, illustrated in Figure 3D,E.

claims.claim: PPTg activity evolves from representing information about the previous trial to representing information about the current trial.
claims.source: These analyses show how PPTg activity evolves from representing information about the previous trial to representing information about the current trial, which may reflect the transfer of previous-trial information from the PPTg to a downstream region where it can be integrated with sensory evidence in order to form a motor plan.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the regression analyses, with an inference about the functional significance.

claims.claim: The evolution of PPTg activity may reflect the transfer of previous-trial information from the PPTg to a downstream region where it can be integrated with sensory evidence to form a motor plan.
claims.source: These analyses show how PPTg activity evolves from representing information about the previous trial to representing information about the current trial, which may reflect the transfer of previous-trial information from the PPTg to a downstream region where it can be integrated with sensory evidence in order to form a motor plan.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the temporal dynamics of neural activity.

claims.claim: Many more PPTg neurons exhibited a significantly positive slope than negative slope in the relationship between firing rate and current choice on ambiguous trials.
claims.source: Across this population of neurons, many more exhibited a significantly positive slope than negative slope (p<0.05, Monte Carlo permutation test; positive slopes: 136/378; negative slopes: 30/378; positive > negative, p=0.001, χ2 test; Figure 4B), indicating a similar relationship between firing rate and current choice as shown in Figure 4A.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the relationship between neural activity and choice, illustrated in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Each mouse exhibited more PPTg neurons with positive than negative slopes in the relationship between firing rate and current choice.
claims.source: To determine whether this was the case, we examined the distribution of slopes separately for each mouse and found that each exhibited more neurons with positive than negative slopes (Figure 4C), even though the behavior of some mice did not depend on previous choice (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the relationship between neural activity and choice, illustrated in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The representation of the choice on the previous trial can directly influence the choice made by the mouse on the current trial.
claims.source: These results suggest that the representation of the choice on the previous trial (Figure 2) can directly influence the choice made by the mouse on the current trial.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the analysis showing that neural activity predicts choice even in mice whose behavior does not depend on previous choice.

claims.claim: Unilateral PPTg inactivation resulted in choices biased ipsilateral to the inactivated PPTg.
claims.source: We found that choices were biased ipsilateral to the inactivated PPTg, as compared to the preceding and following control sessions in which saline was infused to the same PPTg (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the pharmacological inactivation experiments, illustrated in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Unilaterally inactivating the PPTg resulted in a modest ipsilateral influence on choices.
claims.source: We found that unilaterally inactivating the PPTg resulted in a modest ipsilateral influence on choices (Figure 5B; p<0.05, two-tailed unpaired Student's t test, pooled across 3 animals and 30 sets of sessions (424 ± 105 trials; mean ± STD); βMuscimol > 0 in 14/30 individual sets of sessions, βMuscimol < 0 in 6/30 individual sets of sessions, p<0.05, two-tailed one-sample Student's t test; black bars), indicating a causal relationship between PPTg activity and contralateral movements in this task.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the pharmacological inactivation experiments, illustrated in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: There is a causal relationship between PPTg activity and contralateral movements in the odor-guided spatial choice task.
claims.source: We found that unilaterally inactivating the PPTg resulted in a modest ipsilateral influence on choices (Figure 5B; p<0.05, two-tailed unpaired Student's t test, pooled across 3 animals and 30 sets of sessions (424 ± 105 trials; mean ± STD); βMuscimol > 0 in 14/30 individual sets of sessions, βMuscimol < 0 in 6/30 individual sets of sessions, p<0.05, two-tailed one-sample Student's t test; black bars), indicating a causal relationship between PPTg activity and contralateral movements in this task.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the pharmacological inactivation experiments.

claims.claim: Movement latency and duration were longer in muscimol than in saline sessions.
claims.source: Consistent with the modest but significant effect of unilateral inactivation on choice bias, we found that movement latency and duration – both to and from the reward port – were longer in muscimol than in saline sessions, even when contralateral and ipsilateral choices were pooled (Materials and methods; p=4.55 × 10−20, 5.24 × 10−32, and 0.0026, respectively, two-tailed unpaired Student's t tests).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of movement timing in the pharmacological inactivation experiments.

claims.claim: PPTg activity representing previous experience influences action selection.
claims.source: These results support our hypothesis that the PPTg activity representing previous experience (Figure 2) influences action selection.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the pharmacological inactivation experiments.

claims.claim: Behavior in the stimulus-cued spatial-choice task can be accounted for by a Bayesian framework in which choices are influenced by both recent trial history and the sensory stimulus.
claims.source: We first found that behavior in a stimulus-cued spatial-choice task can be accounted for by a Bayesian framework (among others) in which choices are influenced by both recent trial history and the sensory stimulus (Figure 1), consistent with previous studies (Gold et al., 2008; Busse et al., 2011; Akaishi et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the behavioral analyses, supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Activity of a subpopulation of PPTg neurons reflects choices and outcomes in the recent past and correlated with upcoming choice.
claims.source: We then found that activity of a subpopulation of PPTg neurons reflects choices and outcomes in the recent past (Figures 2 and 3) and correlated with upcoming choice (Figure 4), suggesting a role in mediating the influence of recent experience on behavior.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the electrophysiological analyses.

claims.claim: The PPTg encodes representations of recent experience that can contribute to action selection.
claims.source: Together, our results demonstrate that the PPTg encodes representations of recent experience that can contribute to action selection.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from all the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The motor-related role of the PPTg has traditionally been considered in the context of central pattern generation.
claims.source: The motor-related role of the PPTg has traditionally been considered in the context of central pattern generation (Garcia-Rill, 1991).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: PPTg activity encodes specific actions and reflects their outcomes.
claims.source: More recent studies in behaving animals have found that PPTg activity encodes specific actions and reflects their outcomes (Matsumura et al., 1997; Dormont et al., 1998; Okada and Kobayashi, 2009; Norton et al., 2011; Maclaren et al., 2013; Thompson and Felsen, 2013) and have suggested that the PPTg may be involved in attention and other cognitive processes (Steckler et al., 1994; Winn, 2008).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The PPTg may be involved in attention and other cognitive processes.
claims.source: More recent studies in behaving animals have found that PPTg activity encodes specific actions and reflects their outcomes (Matsumura et al., 1997; Dormont et al., 1998; Okada and Kobayashi, 2009; Norton et al., 2011; Maclaren et al., 2013; Thompson and Felsen, 2013) and have suggested that the PPTg may be involved in attention and other cognitive processes (Steckler et al., 1994; Winn, 2008).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: PPTg output may play a role in providing information about recent actions and their outcomes that can be used to guide the selection of actions mediated by downstream motor circuits.
claims.source: The results described here are consistent with these findings and suggest that PPTg output may play a role in providing information about recent actions and their outcomes that can be used to guide the selection of actions mediated by downstream motor circuits.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, involving speculation about the functional role of PPTg.

claims.claim: Downstream circuits do not necessarily utilize PPTg information about recent experience, given that it is represented in PPTg activity even in mice that do not exhibit a behavioral dependence on previous choice.
claims.source: However, downstream circuits do not necessarily utilize this information, given that it is represented in PPTg activity even in mice that do not exhibit a behavioral dependence on previous choice (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the observation that neural representations exist even when behavior does not depend on previous choice.

claims.claim: The PPTg projects to several motor-related regions including other brainstem nuclei and the striatum.
claims.source: While the PPTg projects to several motor-related regions including other brainstem nuclei and the striatum (Beninato and Spencer, 1987; Inglis and Winn, 1995), and the current study cannot rule out the involvement of these regions, an attractive candidate is the SC.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: The SC is an attractive candidate for where PPTg representations of recent experience might be conveyed to modulate action selection.
claims.source: While the PPTg projects to several motor-related regions including other brainstem nuclei and the striatum (Beninato and Spencer, 1987; Inglis and Winn, 1995), and the current study cannot rule out the involvement of these regions, an attractive candidate is the SC.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the downstream target of PPTg projections.

claims.claim: Cholinergic PPTg neurons project to and excite neurons in the SC responsible for motor output.
claims.source: Cholinergic PPTg neurons project to and excite neurons in the SC responsible for motor output (Beninato and Spencer, 1986; Sooksawate et al., 2008; Stubblefield et al., 2015), and nicotinic signaling in the SC has been shown to modulate orienting behavior (Weldon et al., 1983; Aizawa et al., 1999; Watanabe et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous anatomical and physiological studies.

claims.claim: Nicotinic signaling in the SC has been shown to modulate orienting behavior.
claims.source: Cholinergic PPTg neurons project to and excite neurons in the SC responsible for motor output (Beninato and Spencer, 1986; Sooksawate et al., 2008; Stubblefield et al., 2015), and nicotinic signaling in the SC has been shown to modulate orienting behavior (Weldon et al., 1983; Aizawa et al., 1999; Watanabe et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The SC is thought to integrate a wide range of inputs in order to select orienting actions.
claims.source: The SC is thought to integrate a wide range of inputs in order to select orienting actions (Kobayashi and Isa, 2002; Krauzlis et al., 2004; Grossberg et al., 2015; Wolf et al., 2015) and is thus well-positioned to combine – possibly additively – incoming sensory information with prior representations of action value (provided before, during, or even after the onset of sensory input; Figure 3B,C) in order to select the most valuable action (Trappenberg et al., 2001; Dorris et al., 2007; Kim and Basso, 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The SC is well-positioned to combine incoming sensory information with prior representations of action value to select the most valuable action.
claims.source: The SC is thought to integrate a wide range of inputs in order to select orienting actions (Kobayashi and Isa, 2002; Krauzlis et al., 2004; Grossberg et al., 2015; Wolf et al., 2015) and is thus well-positioned to combine – possibly additively – incoming sensory information with prior representations of action value (provided before, during, or even after the onset of sensory input; Figure 3B,C) in order to select the most valuable action (Trappenberg et al., 2001; Dorris et al., 2007; Kim and Basso, 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work and inference from the temporal dynamics shown in Figure 3B,C.

claims.claim: The source of prior representations of action value in the SC may be the PPTg.
claims.source: Our results suggest that the source of these prior representations may be the PPTg, which could complement other SC inputs – such as inhibition from the basal ganglia (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1983; Chevalier et al., 1985) – in biasing action selection by modulating SC processing according to recently-experienced action-value associations (Kobayashi and Isa, 2002; Hikosaka et al., 2006; Wolf et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings about the functional role of PPTg input to SC.

claims.claim: PPTg input could complement other SC inputs, such as inhibition from the basal ganglia, in biasing action selection.
claims.source: Our results suggest that the source of these prior representations may be the PPTg, which could complement other SC inputs – such as inhibition from the basal ganglia (Hikosaka and Wurtz, 1983; Chevalier et al., 1985) – in biasing action selection by modulating SC processing according to recently-experienced action-value associations (Kobayashi and Isa, 2002; Hikosaka et al., 2006; Wolf et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, supported by citations to previous work on basal ganglia-SC interactions.

claims.claim: Representations of trial history similar to that in PPTg have been observed in the striatum, prefrontal cortex, and premotor cortex.
claims.source: Given the importance of trial history for action selection, it is not surprising that representations of trial history similar to that shown here have been observed in several brain areas, including the striatum (Lau and Glimcher, 2007, 2008; Histed et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2013), prefrontal cortex (Histed et al., 2009) and premotor cortex (Marcos et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Activity in the striatum, prefrontal cortex, and premotor cortex typically reflects information from several previous trials.
claims.source: Activity in these regions typically reflects information from several previous trials, while PPTg activity was primarily associated with the immediately preceding trial (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This statement contrasts the findings in PPTg with previous work in other brain regions, drawing on established knowledge.

claims.claim: PPTg activity was primarily associated with the immediately preceding trial.
claims.source: Activity in these regions typically reflects information from several previous trials, while PPTg activity was primarily associated with the immediately preceding trial (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the preference analysis, illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The representations in the PPTg suggest a complementary mechanism to the more computationally expensive processing in other regions for integrating internal representations of experience with sensory evidence.

results.result: Behavioral choices in the odor-guided spatial choice task are influenced by the choice and outcome on the previous trial, but not by events from two trials back. Mice tended to repeat the same choice as on the previous trial, especially when rewarded, and this influence was not explained by movement duration differences.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C25 collectively demonstrate that behavior depends on the immediately preceding trial through multiple converging lines of evidence: psychometric analysis (C17-C18), logistic regression showing positive β coefficients for previous choice (C19-C20), model comparison showing improved prediction with 1-trial-back but not 2-trials-back information (C21-C22), and control analysis ruling out movement duration confounds (C23). The statistical tests are appropriate and significant.

results.result: During the pre-stimulus epoch, a large fraction of PPTg neurons (75% for choice, 46% for outcome) exhibited selectivity for the choice and outcome on the previous trial, but few neurons showed selectivity for the current trial or for events two trials back. More neurons preferred contralateral than ipsilateral previous choices.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C37 provide strong evidence from ROC-based preference analysis with appropriate Monte Carlo permutation tests (p<0.05). The finding that 75% of neurons show previous-trial selectivity while few show current-trial or 2-trials-back selectivity is statistically robust (Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA with post-hoc comparisons, p-values ranging from 10^-30 to 10^-4). The contralateral bias (49% vs 26%, p=0.001, χ² test) is also well-supported.

results.result: Two-thirds of PPTg neurons maintained their preference for which reward port was chosen during movements in opposite directions (to and from the reward port), suggesting that neural activity reflects choice rather than movement direction per se.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 address a critical confound through an appropriate control analysis. The finding that 2/3 of neurons maintain port preference across opposite movement directions (p=9.12×10^-6, χ² test) provides strong evidence that the neural representation is choice-based rather than purely motor. However, the authors appropriately note this cannot entirely rule out body position effects.

results.result: PPTg neural activity evolves over the trial from representing previous-trial information (choice and outcome) early in the trial to representing current-trial information later. Previous choice representation persists longer than previous outcome representation, with some neurons continuing to reflect previous choice even after the current choice is made.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C49 describe temporal dynamics using linear regression analysis with appropriate time-binning (100ms bins, 10ms steps). The regression coefficients (β^1_Choice, β^0_Choice, β^1_Outcome, β^0_Outcome) show clear temporal evolution illustrated in Figure 3. The analysis is performed on neurons pre-selected for previous-choice preference (378/506 neurons), which is appropriate but creates a selection bias acknowledged for outcome analysis (C48).

results.result: On ambiguous trials, PPTg firing rates during the pre-stimulus epoch predicted upcoming choice: neurons with higher firing rates were more likely to be followed by choices matching their previous-trial preference. This relationship held even in individual mice whose behavior did not depend on previous choice, suggesting a direct neural influence on choice.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 demonstrate a trial-by-trial correlation between neural activity and behavior. The finding that 136/378 neurons showed significant positive slopes vs 30/378 negative slopes (p=0.001, χ² test) is robust. Critically, C52 shows this pattern holds within each mouse individually, even those without behavioral dependence on previous choice (Figure 1E), strengthening the causal inference in C53. Monte Carlo permutation tests appropriately assess significance.

results.result: Unilateral pharmacological inactivation of PPTg with muscimol produced a modest but significant ipsilateral bias in choices and increased movement latency and duration, indicating a causal role for PPTg in contralateral movement selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 provide causal evidence through pharmacological manipulation. The ipsilateral bias (β_Muscimol > 0 in 14/30 sessions, p<0.05) and increased movement times (p=4.55×10^-20, 5.24×10^-32, 0.0026) are statistically significant. However, the effect size is modest, and only 14/30 sessions showed the predicted direction individually. The use of within-subject controls (pre- and post-saline sessions) strengthens the design.

results.result: PPTg inactivation decreased the influence of previous choice on current choice (β^1_Choice was lower in muscimol vs saline sessions, p=0.021), causally linking PPTg activity to the behavioral influence of recent experience.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C16, and C61 provide the key causal link between PPTg activity and history-dependent behavior. The finding that β^1_Choice decreased with muscimol (p=0.021, one-tailed Mann-Whitney U test) directly supports the hypothesis. However, the effect is modest and the one-tailed test suggests a directional hypothesis. The result is consistent with the neural recording data but would benefit from replication.

results.result: PPTg neurons encode representations of recent choices and outcomes that predict and contribute to upcoming action selection, providing a neural substrate for incorporating recent experience into decision-making.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C14-C15, C63-C64 represent the main conclusions synthesizing the behavioral, neural recording, and causal manipulation data. The evidence is strong: neural selectivity for previous trials (C3, C14), prediction of upcoming choice (C4, C15), and causal effects of inactivation (addressed in other result groups). The convergence of correlational and causal evidence supports these summary claims.

results.result: There is a modest positive correlation (r=0.25, p=1.42×10^-8) between neural preference for choice on the previous trial and preference for choice on the current trial.
results.evaluation: Claim C31 reports a statistically significant but weak correlation. The p-value is highly significant due to large sample size (506 neurons), but the correlation coefficient of 0.25 indicates only 6.25% shared variance. This suggests some neurons maintain choice selectivity across trials, but most do not, which is consistent with the temporal dynamics shown in Figure 3.

results.result: The authors propose that PPTg provides a simple mechanism for incorporating recent experience into action selection by conveying previous-trial information to downstream motor regions (particularly SC) where it can be integrated with sensory evidence, though downstream circuits may not always utilize this information.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C50, C68-C69, C71, C76-C77, C81-C82 represent mechanistic interpretations and speculation about circuit function. While the PPTg→SC projection is anatomically established (C11, C72), the specific functional role proposed here is not directly tested. The observation that neural representations exist even without behavioral dependence (C69) actually weakens the proposed mechanism. These claims require additional experiments (e.g., SC recordings during PPTg manipulation, pathway-specific manipulations).

results.result: Behavior in the task can be accounted for by a Bayesian framework in which choices are influenced by both recent trial history and sensory stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 invokes a Bayesian framework, but the manuscript does not actually implement or test a Bayesian model. The logistic regression model used is consistent with but does not uniquely support a Bayesian interpretation. The authors acknowledge the framework 'may be imperfect' given that optimal performance should not depend on previous trials. The claim overstates the evidence for a specific computational framework.

results.result: The study recorded from 506 PPTg neurons across seven mice (three C57BL/6J and four ChAT-Cre) for electrophysiology, and used three C57BL/6J mice for pharmacology experiments, with no observed differences between mouse strains.
results.evaluation: Claims C88, C93-C96 describe the sample sizes and subjects. The numbers are clearly stated and appropriate for the analyses performed. However, the claim of 'no differences across backgrounds' (C96) is stated without supporting statistical analysis or data presentation, which is a minor weakness in reporting.

results.result: The manuscript situates the work within established knowledge about action selection, Bayesian integration, striatal circuits, PPTg-SC connectivity, and prior observations of trial history effects across species and brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C12, C38, C65-C67, C70, C72-C75, C78-C79, C84, C86-C87 represent background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These claims accurately represent prior work and provide necessary context. The citations appear appropriate and the characterizations of previous findings are reasonable, though detailed verification of each cited claim is beyond this review's scope.
